llm.summary: The skill appears to be a real here.now publishing integration, but it needs Review because it has agents store account API keys locally and includes broad private Drive sharing and deletion abilities beyond the top-level publishing framing.

dimensions.detail: Network uploads to here.now, local file reads for selected publish/import targets, and local state writes fit the stated service, but users should treat publish, Drive import/export, and custom API base options as sensitive operations.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The install guidance is a normal npx skills add command; no postinstall hooks, hidden startup mechanism, or automatic background execution were found in the inspected artifact.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The activation phrases are broad for a publishing tool, and publishing defaults to link-accessible sites, but the skill does disclose live URLs, access modes, workspace behavior, and Drive privacy guidance in the instructions.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The skill instructs agents to collect sign-in codes, receive API keys, and immediately persist them in ~/.herenow/credentials; it also creates scoped Drive tokens and writes claim tokens to .herenow/state.json.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: Publishing files and sites to live URLs is coherent and clearly central, but the artifact also includes private Drive storage, token sharing, import/export, rm/delete, profile and broader account-management references that are only introduced later in the skill body.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable letting the agent publish selected files to live here.now URLs, manage private Drive content, create share tokens, and store a here.now API key under ~/.herenow/credentials. Avoid using the Drive share/delete/import/export and custom base URL options unless you explicitly intend those actions, and do not provide sensitive content unless the target visibility is clear.
llm.findings:
[TP4] unexpected: Accepted in part: Drive management is present and powerful, while the frontmatter mainly frames the skill as website and file publishing; the body discloses Drive later, so this is under-disclosure rather than evidence of malicious behavior.
[SDI-2] unexpected: Accepted in part for Drive workflows: private storage, sharing tokens, recursive import/export, and deletion are real capabilities and exceed a narrow publish-only purpose, though they are documented in the skill.
[SDI-2] expected: Accepted as a Review concern for credentials: account API keys are expected for permanent sites and workspaces, but the skill directs the agent to handle sign-in codes and save returned API keys locally without a separate consent gate.
[SQP-1] expected: Downgraded: phrases like sharing and generating a URL are expected for a publishing skill, but the broad triggers increase the need for user confirmation before exposing sensitive content.
[SQP-2] expected: Mostly downgraded: the artifact repeatedly says publishing creates live URLs and states the default access mode, though users should still be warned before public or team-accessible publication.
[SSD-3] expected: Accepted as a Review concern: local credential storage is disclosed and chmod 600 is recommended, but immediate agent-managed persistence of a long-lived API key is high-impact.
[SSD-3] expected: Accepted as a Review concern: the one-time code exchange is an authentication workflow for the service, but it makes the agent a credential-custody path.
[E1] expected: Downgraded: uploading selected local files to server-provided upload URLs is expected for publishing; lack of upload URL validation is a hardening gap, especially with custom API bases, but not artifact-backed exfiltration.
[E1] expected: Downgraded in part: finalizing via a server-provided URL is part of the publish flow, but sending authorization headers to an unvalidated response URL is a real implementation risk if the API endpoint is compromised or overridden.
